description: Interested in learning about 3d visualizations and utilizing space data.
summary:
LunaSol is an interactive web tool that shows mission planners what the sky looks like from any lunar landing site on any date. At the Moon's south pole, the Sun never rises more than about 1.5 degress above the horizon and Earth orbits low, so a distant ridge can cut a lander's power or its radio link. A few kilometres and a few days can change everything about a mission.

LunaSol combines NASA data in one view: JPL Horizons for the positions of the Sun and Earth, and LOLA laser altimetry for the terrain. For each site it shows a 360° horizon view, live terrain shadows and a 3D landscape, then calculates hours of sunlight and Earth contact, the longest night, and a GO / BORDERLINE / NO-GO verdict against adjustable mission limits. Planners can compare sites side by side, see what happens if the landing date slips, and find the best landing windows. Its Sun and Earth positions match direct JPL Horizons queries to within 0.007°.

Existing NASA tools answer these questions separately and need specialists. LunaSol aggregates them so science and engineering teams can decide from the same picture, and hobbyists/students can learn the challenges of lunar landings in the south pole.
details:
What it does

LunaSol answers the big question every lunar mission planner faces: if we land at this site on this date, how many hours can the lander work and talk to Earth, how long is its longest night, and what changes if the schedule slips?

Users pick a site from 26 curated locations (Artemis III candidate regions, commercial and international landers, Apollo sites) or click anywhere on the Moon. LunaSol then shows:

  • Horizon view: a 360° panorama from the landing site, with the real terrain skyline and the paths of the Sun and Earth across the mission.
  • Live shadow map: a map of the south pole whose shadows sweep across craters as time plays.
  • 3D terrain: the landscape around the site, lit by the Sun at that moment, including a view from the lander itself.
  • Verdicts: a GO / BORDERLINE / NO-GO result against mission limits (battery survival, hours of power and Earth contact per day, longest communication gap), with the deciding limit named in plain words.
  • What if: the same mission re-evaluated for landing up to 15 days early or 30 days late, the best landing dates over the next 300 days, and a science-versus-operations comparison.
  • Timeline and comparison: up to three sites side by side, built by dragging sites onto the timeline as in a video editor.

How it works

Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons: hourly points on the Moon directly beneath each body, from November 2026 to January 2031. From these, LunaSol computes where the Sun and Earth appear from any site, including the small offset from standing on the surface. We validated this against direct Horizons queries for four sites; the largest difference was 0.007°, about 1% of the Sun's width.

Terrain comes from LOLA, the laser altimeter on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (80 m per pixel at the south pole). For each site we trace the terrain outward 400 km in 1,440 directions, including the Moon's curvature, to find the true horizon. Sunlight is measured as the fraction of the Sun's disc above that horizon, so power rises and falls gradually instead of switching on and off. Shadows on the maps are computed on the graphics card by tracing a line from each point toward the Sun across the terrain.

Tools

  • Web app: TypeScript, React and Vite; three.js and WebGL shaders for 3D and shadows; SVG for charts.
  • Data pipeline: Python and NumPy, querying the JPL Horizons API and processing LOLA data from NASA's Planetary Data System.
  • Hosting: deployed on Vercel as a static site, so it needs no server and works offline once loaded.
  • Testing: 28 automated tests that check the astronomy, the verdict logic, and the guided tour's facts against the real data.

Benefits and impact

NASA's tools (Horizons, Quickmap, Moon Trek) are powerful but separate, and they need specialists. Scientists at NASA may also be at odds with Engineers when it comes to picking a location, raising questions that concerns the research value of the site. LunaSol puts their answers in one screen that a mission planner, a scientist or a student can read in seconds. Science and engineering teams can argue from the same picture: everyone can see why a scientifically valuable site fails on battery life, and whether a two-week slip saves it. Shareable links reopen the exact scenario for a colleague.

Creativity

  • A sky-first design: the horizon view is the center of the screen, because the sky decides the mission.
  • A video-editor layout (sites as clips, a timeline of tracks, a preview, an inspector) that technical and non-technical users already understand.
  • A GO map that colors the ground itself by verdict for the chosen date, and a lander's-eye 3D view.
  • Simple and Expert modes: plain language for newcomers, every angle and number for specialists.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and honesty: every number traces to NASA data. Approximate results (dates outside the data range, estimated site coordinates, team-assigned science scores) are labelled.
  • Accessibility: verdicts never rely on color alone, every chart has text equivalents, the tool works by keyboard, and it respects reduced-motion settings.
  • Limits we document: the terrain grid is 80 m, so features smaller than that aren't in the horizon, and the power model does not simulate battery charge or temperature as the engineering of rovers and landers are often confidential.
